doc.title: Ingrid Sertso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: World turmoil, angry free players, and the demonic music business
summary: Hard times drive creative need; anger is ego and lifestyle; Whitney Houston and Jimi Hendrix show exploitation.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Along those same lines, you know on my drive down here I listened to the news on NPR a couple of times. And there is so much serious turmoil in the world, it just seems, well I can’t even describe how it seems. But is your creative process affected by what’s going on around you? Even locally or world wide?

Well it puts you more into music. The worse one side gets, the economy and politics and so on, government, the more musicians jump up. Because the more the need is there for creative expression. So the worse it gets the more we need to do music you know. In terms of effecting us, what’s happening in Iraq and Russia and so on, I don’t know. I wouldn’t know whether we would express that in the music. Probably unconsciously it would be woven in also. It’s not consciously otherwise it would be totally negative, no.
I know there’s been a few instances of critics describing some of the free players, Archie Shepp and so forth, as sounding very angry.
Do you think they were angry most of the time? I don’t know if that’s a fair question or not.

It’s all an ego thing. It’s all an ego thing. Yeah. It has to do with lifestyle, it has to do with no money, it has to do with the way the musicians are treated. And if you don’t work on it you become really angry you know. The music business is horrible. It’s demonic.

Demonic. When Whitney Houston died, Whitney Houston? I totally adored her. She was, for me, the purist Gospel singer. Total purity. I cried almost every time I heard her. When she died the African singer, what’s her name, went on CNN and she said, “The music business is demonic.”
I know who you’re talking about but I can’t think of her name.

Yeah I can’t remember her name. And once they have you, they discover your talent, they have you. They get you. It’s like I picked up a journal, a newspaper in a coffee shop in Europe, and they were writing about Jimi Hendrix. The advantage the managers, the producers, made off Jimi Hendrix is unbelievable. At the end, where he really made a lot of money, they only gave him a stipend for a week. Sometimes because he needed acid, to buy acid, he slept in a park instead of in a hotel. So it’s — and he was a very good hearted person. Very, very good hearted. And if you don’t work on it, you are angry. I don’t know how we do it. All our lives we make only money on music. Only. Only money on music. We only make a living on music.
I was going to ask that. You know you have it in common with a lot of jazz musicians.
And you have to work not to become angry.
